speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: DRY isn't about never writing similar-looking code. It's about never duplicating the same piece of knowledge.

beats.content: DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. The rule is that every piece of business logic should live in exactly one place. If the same validation rule exists in three services, a rule change means finding all three, and you'll miss one eventually.

The fix is extraction. Email validation logic in both UserService and OrderService becomes a shared EmailValidator utility. Both services call it. Now the rule lives in one place, and changing it once is enough.

candidates miss: DRY is about knowledge duplication, not code that looks similar. Two methods that happen to be three lines and look alike are not necessarily a DRY violation if they represent different rules that will evolve separately. Forcing them into a shared abstraction too early creates coupling. That's why over-applying DRY is just as bad as ignoring it.

speakable_v2.cap: DRY: one source of truth for each piece of logic. If a rule changes, it should change in exactly one place.
followup_handoff: Can DRY be over-applied? When does abstraction hurt?

question: What does DRY mean and how do you apply it?
title: DRY — Do Not Repeat Yourself principle
direct_answer: **DRY** stands for **Don't Repeat Yourself**. Every piece of knowledge should have a **single, authoritative representation** in the codebase. If the same logic appears in two places, a change to that logic requires updates in two places — one is often missed, causing bugs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand DRY as being about knowledge duplication, not just code duplication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Over-applying DRY to create over-abstracted code just to avoid any repetition — accidental similarity is not DRY violation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that WET (Write Everything Twice / We Enjoy Typing) is the antipattern, and that DRY applies to logic not just text

speakable_v2.hook: KISS is one of the hardest principles to follow because simple solutions feel less impressive than clever ones.

beats.content: KISS stands for Keep It Simple. The principle says the simplest solution that correctly solves the problem is usually the best one. Complexity should earn its place by solving a real problem, not by showing off what you know.

content: Using a design pattern when a plain method would work is a KISS violation
A stream chain nobody can read at a glance is a KISS violation
A 50-line solution to a problem that needs 5 lines is a KISS violation

beats.content: non-obvious: KISS isn't lazy coding. Writing simple code is actually harder than writing complex code. It requires really understanding the problem, resisting the temptation to over-engineer, and trusting that future changes will be handled when they're needed, not speculatively.

speakable_v2.cap: Complexity should justify itself. If a simpler solution works, use it. Your teammates will thank you during the 3 AM incident.
followup_handoff: How do you balance KISS with good design patterns?

question: What does KISS mean and why does it matter?
title: KISS — Keep It Simple, Stupid principle
direct_answer: **KISS** stands for **Keep It Simple, Stupid** (or Keep It Short and Simple). It says: **the simplest solution that works is usually the best**. Over-engineering, premature abstraction, and complex design patterns where they are not needed make code harder to read, debug, and maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you value simplicity and can recognize over-engineering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking KISS means lazy coding — it means intentional simplicity, which is actually harder to achieve
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Quote Antoine de Saint-Exupery: perfection is achieved not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away

sections.title: Simple vs complex
sections.content: A KISS violation looks like: using a design pattern when a simple method would do, creating abstract factory chains for objects that are never swapped, writing 50 lines when 5 would work, or using lambda + stream chains so complex that nobody can read them. The test: can a new developer understand this code in 5 minutes? If not, it probably violates KISS.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: KISS means prefer the simplest solution that solves the problem. In practice, this means I avoid adding design patterns just because I know them, avoid abstracting things that are only used once, and prefer readable code over clever code. If a simple if-else statement solves the problem and does not need to be extended, there is no reason to introduce a Strategy pattern. Complexity should earn its place — it should solve a real problem.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: The most expensive code to maintain is code that does something nobody needed.

beats.content: YAGNI stands for You Aren't Gonna Need It. The principle says: don't implement a feature until you actually have a requirement for it. Every line of code you add must be maintained, tested, and understood by everyone who works on the codebase.

A classic YAGNI violation is building a plugin architecture for a payment system when there's only one payment provider and no plans for more. You spent two weeks building something nobody asked for, it adds complexity, and requirements change anyway so it may never be used.

sharp edge: YAGNI isn't about not thinking ahead. You still design your code to be extensible. But extensible design doesn't mean implementing all possible extensions now. It means writing code that's easy to extend later, when the requirement is actually real.

speakable_v2.cap: YAGNI: build what's needed today. Design for extensibility, but don't implement extensions until you need them.
followup_handoff: How does YAGNI relate to technical debt?

question: What does YAGNI mean and when should you apply it?
title: YAGNI — You Aren't Gonna Need It principle
direct_answer: **YAGNI** stands for **You Aren't Gonna Need It**. Do not add functionality until you actually need it. Building features for hypothetical future requirements that may never arrive wastes time, adds untested code, and makes the codebase harder to understand. Build what is needed today.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the cost of speculative features
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing YAGNI with do not plan ahead — YAGNI is about not implementing features, not about not thinking ahead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect YAGNI to agile and iterative development — build, ship, learn, then add the next thing

sections.title: YAGNI in practice
sections.content: YAGNI violations look like: adding support for multiple databases when only MySQL is needed, building a plugin architecture when there is one use case, adding configuration flags that will never be used, or writing XML-driven extensibility when the feature is a one-off. All of this code must be maintained, tested, and documented — forever — even if no one ever uses it.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: YAGNI says: do not build it until you need it. It is very tempting to say, what if we need to support multiple payment providers in the future — I will build a plugin architecture now. But if you never need it, you have spent time building something that adds complexity without adding value. In agile development, the better approach is to build what is needed now, ship it, get feedback, and add the next thing when the requirement is real.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: DRY, KISS, and YAGNI are three lenses on the same goal: write just enough clean code to solve today's problem.

beats.content: They address different dimensions but point in the same direction. DRY keeps logic consolidated and maintainable. KISS keeps it readable and understandable. YAGNI keeps the scope minimal. Together they mean: write the simplest non-duplicated code that does exactly what's needed now.

non-obvious: they can tension each other. Aggressively applying DRY can violate KISS by over-abstracting. Aggressively applying KISS can delay DRY refactoring. Good engineering judgment is knowing when each principle should win.

speakable_v2.cap: All three principles push toward the same philosophy: minimal, readable, no-repetition code that solves today's actual problem.
followup_handoff: How do these principles apply to API design?

question: How do DRY, KISS, and YAGNI work together?
title: DRY + KISS + YAGNI — how the three principles complement each other
direct_answer: They address **different dimensions of code quality**: DRY avoids knowledge duplication (maintainability), KISS avoids unnecessary complexity (readability), YAGNI avoids premature features (simplicity over time). Together they push toward code that is **minimal, readable, and does not repeat itself**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to see the relationship between the three principles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating them as three separate unrelated rules
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a single code example that violates all three and explain which part violates which principle

sections.content:

| KISS | Keep It Simple | Complexity that hides intent | 5-layer abstraction for a one-off feature |
| YAGNI | You Aren't Gonna Need It | Wasted effort on speculative features | Plugin system nobody asked for |

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: The three principles complement each other. DRY is about not duplicating logic — same code in two places is a maintenance risk. KISS is about not over-complicating — the simplest solution that works is preferred. YAGNI is about not building ahead of requirements — do not add features until they are needed. Together they point to the same philosophy: write just enough clean code to solve today's problem, no more, no less.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 Spring Boot app applying SOLID principles
speakable_v2.hook: Extracting a shared abstraction from two methods that look the same today but mean different things is worse than duplication.

beats.content: DRY can be over-applied when you confuse accidental similarity with real duplication. Two methods that happen to look alike right now aren't necessarily representing the same knowledge. They might evolve in completely different directions.

If you extract them into a shared utility prematurely, you've coupled two unrelated concerns. When one needs to change, you're forced to also affect the other, or you add awkward flags to distinguish the cases. The coupling is worse than the original duplication.

production trap: the practical rule is the Rule of Three. See it once: leave it. See it twice: be cautious, maybe a coincidence. See it three times with the same intent: extract it. This prevents over-abstraction while still catching true duplication early enough to matter.

speakable_v2.cap: The Rule of Three: duplicate once, abstract on the third. Two occurrences might just be coincidence. Three with the same intent are DRY violation.

question: Can DRY be over-applied? When does abstraction hurt?
title: When DRY goes too far — premature abstraction
direct_answer: Yes. **Over-applying DRY** leads to premature abstraction — creating shared utilities for code that happens to look similar but serves different purposes. If two pieces of code are accidentally similar today but will evolve differently, forcing them into a shared abstraction creates coupling that hurts later. The **Rule of Three** is a practical guide: duplicate once, abstract on the third occurrence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Nuanced understanding that principles are guidelines, not absolutes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating DRY as a law that must always be followed, leading to over-abstracted code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Rule of Three and WET (Write Everything Twice) as a pragmatic approach

sections.title: Accidental duplication vs real duplication
sections.content: Not all code that looks the same represents the same knowledge. If UserService and OrderService both have a 3-line validation method that happens to look similar today, but one will grow to include business rules about users and the other about orders — unifying them now couples two unrelated things. When one changes, it breaks the other. The Rule of Three: see it once, note it; see it twice, be cautious; see it three times in three places with the same intent, extract it.

sections.title: How to say this in an interview
sections.content: DRY can be over-applied. If I see two methods that look similar and immediately extract them into a shared abstraction, I might be coupling things that only look the same today. If those two pieces of code serve different concerns and will evolve differently, my abstraction becomes a bottleneck. The practical rule I follow is the Rule of Three — if I see the same thing three times with the same intent, it is worth extracting. Seeing it twice might just be a coincidence.
